title: The One With The Kips

jokes.text: "But it's dark out." / "That's because you always sleep till noon, silly. This is what nine looks like."
jokes.setup: One character is disoriented waking up at 9 AM, treating darkness as unusual
jokes.punchline: The other explains that 9 AM looks dark because they're used to sleeping until noon — delivered with gentle condescension
jokes.explanation: A light, competent opener that establishes the secret-couple dynamic. The punchline 'This is what nine looks like' has decent specificity and rhythm. Character-appropriate for Monica's slightly bossy warmth. Nothing exceptional but it functions well.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why is it so dark? It's only 9 in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Someone
dialogue.line: Monica, it's 9 at night.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: "We could be naked the entire time." / "All weekend? That's a whole lot of naked."
jokes.setup: Monica pitches a romantic, interruption-free weekend getaway
jokes.punchline: Chandler's response treats the prospect of an entire weekend naked as a logistical quantity to be assessed rather than a romantic given
jokes.explanation: "That's a whole lot of naked" is a funny, Chandler-specific line — his instinct to quantify and slightly deflate romantic enthusiasm is core to his character. Economical and well-delivered in context.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's called winter. The sun comes up later. It's science.

jokes.text: "I wanted to go to this culinary fair in Jersey!" / "Okay. You know you're not, though."
jokes.setup: Chandler suggests Monica use a fake "chef thing" as her cover story for the weekend
jokes.punchline: Monica genuinely gets excited about an actual culinary fair in Jersey, before being shut down — she briefly forgot it was a lie
jokes.explanation: Very Monica — her passion for food overtakes her situational awareness mid-lie. Chandler's flat "You know you're not, though" is a perfect deadpan correction. Character-specific and well-structured in a small space.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. The entire weekend? That's like 60 hours!

jokes.text: "How weird! Chandler just said he's got a conference there."
jokes.setup: Monica announces her fake cover story (culinary fair in Jersey) to the group
jokes.punchline: She then "discovers" Chandler coincidentally has a conference in the same place — performing oblivious surprise at her own coordinated lie
jokes.explanation: Monica's performance of surprise is funny because we know the truth. The irony is well-established and the acting carries the joke. Good dramatic irony setup for the audience.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Why don't you guys just go to Connecticut instead? Or Delaware? I hear Delaware's nice.

jokes.text: "That's funny. Seems like Chandler's conference could've been in Connecticut or Vermont."
jokes.setup: Monica announces that Chandler's conference happens to be in the same New Jersey location as her culinary fair
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately clocks the convenient geography with pointed sarcasm — implying he sees through the cover story
jokes.explanation: Ross calling out the flimsy coincidence is a sharp, economical line. The specificity of naming Connecticut or Vermont — real, plausible alternatives — makes it land better than a vague observation would.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're not a couple! We're just two guys who live together, share a bed, and enjoy romantic dinners by candlelight. Perfectly normal!

jokes.text: "I'm not in charge of where the conference is held." / "Do you want people to think it's fake? It's a real conference."
jokes.setup: Ross implies the conference location is suspiciously convenient
jokes.punchline: Chandler defensively insists the fake conference is real — the protest itself is an admission of guilt, and the more he insists, the more absurd it becomes
jokes.explanation: Classic comic over-protest. Chandler's panic-defensive mode is very character-specific. "It's a real conference" lands because of how clearly unconvincing it sounds.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I can't see Rachel when Emily's in town. I just... I can't.

jokes.text: "I'm focusing on the 'I get to see my wife' part... and not on the part that makes me do this." [Ross makes a grimacing/nauseated face]
jokes.setup: Joey points out that if Emily comes, Ross won't be able to see Rachel anymore
jokes.punchline: Ross acknowledges this by physically demonstrating his discomfort — presumably a full-body cringe or gag — rather than processing it verbally
jokes.explanation: "The part that makes me do this" is a great setup for a physical gag — letting the actor's face do the work. It acknowledges emotional complexity while getting a laugh. The structure is elegant: verbal setup, physical punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You flip it over, then you flip it back.

jokes.text: "It doesn't seem like it'll work."
jokes.setup: Ross has just finished explaining his convoluted plan to somehow maintain his marriage while keeping all friendships intact
jokes.punchline: Joey cuts through all of it with a single honest, childlike observation
jokes.explanation: Joey's blunt simplicity cutting through Ross's self-delusion is a classic archetype of his character, and it's deployed perfectly here. Five words doing the work of a paragraph. High economy score is warranted — this is Joey at his most useful comedically.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I flipped my mattress.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, that's a good idea. How come you thought of that?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, you flip your mattress to even out the wear.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh! Oh! That's genius!

jokes.text: "So I'm thinking, basically, we pick it up, and then we flip it." (re: the mattress)
jokes.setup: The gang is flipping Monica's mattress; Chandler is apparently in charge of the plan
jokes.punchline: His "strategy" is simply restating the literal definition of flipping a mattress, delivered with the gravity of an actual plan
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Chandler presenting a tautology as insight. His analytical self-importance deflated by the absolute emptiness of his contribution. Good Chandler beat.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Hey Joey.

jokes.text: "That's better than my way."
jokes.setup: Chandler has just explained that the plan to flip a mattress is to pick it up and flip it
jokes.punchline: Ross implies he had a different, apparently worse method for flipping a mattress — which is an absurd suggestion since there's really only one way
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of implying there's an inferior method of mattress-flipping is the whole joke. Very economical — four words creating an entire implied idiotic scenario. Solid.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Remember Ross's wedding? That disaster taught me something important. If something that catastrophic can happen at a wedding, who knows what else could go wrong? So I've prepared emergency supplies for every possible scenario.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, that was years ago.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Exactly! Which means we're overdue for the next disaster. I'm not taking chances anymore.

jokes.text: Joey hiding behind a mattress as it's flipped, with Rachel's letter from her mom visible — "Oh, look! A letter from my mom."
jokes.setup: The group flips Monica's mattress
jokes.punchline: Joey has apparently been hiding behind/under the mattress, and when it's flipped a letter is revealed — implying Joey has been eavesdropping in an absurdly literal way
jokes.explanation: The mattress flip revealing hidden things is a mild physical gag. The letter is a convenient distraction device more than a punchline, but the moment has light charm.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, I've got a flashlight, batteries, a first aid kit, some water, and granola bars.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What's this?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's a flare gun.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you're gonna shoot me!

jokes.text: "Hey, Joey's ass."
jokes.setup: Joey is pressed against the door trying to hear the conversation in the other room; his backside is facing Chandler
jokes.punchline: Chandler casually greets Joey's rear end as if it's a person — deadpan acknowledgment of a ridiculous physical situation
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum impact. The casualness of "Hey, Joey's ass" — greeting a body part like an acquaintance — is a perfectly Chandler move. Economy score is high because nothing about this joke is wasted.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, what if there's a nuclear holocaust? I'm not gonna have sex in a nuclear holocaust!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And even if I do, I'm not gonna want to repopulate the Earth. That's not a pretty picture, I don't want to spend the rest of my life looking at my son and thinking, 'Nope, should've used a condom on that one.'

jokes.text: Joey's emergency survival kit in Monica's mattress: candy bars, crossword puzzles, Mad Libs, and condoms
jokes.setup: Joey has prepared for being trapped in Monica's apartment by hiding supplies under her mattress
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from snacks (sensible) to crosswords (quirky) to Mad Libs (delightfully childish) to condoms (absurd leap)
jokes.explanation: This is well-constructed escalation comedy. The list builds logically from survival supplies to increasingly strange choices. The condoms are the perfect final beat. Joey's prepper instincts + his id-driven priorities are entirely in character. The reveal that he anticipated this scenario from the last Ross/Rachel incident adds a smart layer.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, if everyone on Earth died, how would the people repopulate?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, theoretically the last man and woman would—

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No no no, but like, if EVERYONE died, then there'd be no one left to, you know, do it with.

jokes.text: "Condoms? You don't know how long we'll be in here. We may have to re-populate the Earth." / "And condoms are the way to do that?"
jokes.setup: Chandler finds condoms in Joey's emergency kit and questions them
jokes.punchline: Joey's justification — that they may need to repopulate the Earth — directly contradicts what condoms are for; Chandler points out this logical impossibility
jokes.explanation: The two-beat structure is excellent: Joey's delusional apocalyptic logic is funny on its own, but Chandler's callback question — pointing out the biological contradiction — earns a second, bigger laugh. Joey genuinely didn't think this through, which is the character. The punchline 'And condoms are the way to do that?' is delivered as straight inquiry, not sarcasm, which makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! Our dog died! / What? / Oh, my God! LaPooh, our dog! / LaPooh's still alive?
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to have a serious conversation with Rachel about Emily's condition; Rachel gets a letter from her mom
jokes.punchline: The dog death completely derails the conversation — and Ross's bewildered 'LaPooh's still alive?' reveals he didn't even know the dog was alive
jokes.explanation: Good comic interruption — using a minor tragedy (dog death) to avoid a major one (the Emily conversation). Ross's clueless 'LaPooh's still alive?' is an unexpected extra laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: LaPooh died? How is that possible? She's only been alive for like three weeks!

jokes.text: "It says he was hit by an ice-cream truck and dragged for... nineteen blocks!"
jokes.setup: Rachel receives a letter about her childhood dog LaPooh dying
jokes.punchline: The death is revealed to be spectacularly, absurdly violent — an ice cream truck dragging a dog 19 blocks is so over-the-top it tips into dark comedy
jokes.explanation: The specific number — nineteen blocks — is what elevates this from generic dark comedy to genuine laugh. It's precise enough to feel written, excessive enough to be absurd. The pause before "nineteen blocks" is a classic timing beat that must land well live.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, what happened to LaPooh?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: He was hit by a bus.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh no! Which bus?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The M15.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Where was he crossing?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: At the corner of 5th and Madison.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What time of day?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Quarter past three on a Tuesday.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Was he wearing his lucky sweater?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The blue one? With the little poodle on it? Yeah.

jokes.text: "Chocolates on the pillows! I love that!" / "You should live with Joey. Rolos everywhere."
jokes.setup: Monica is delighted by hotel chocolates on the pillow — a small romantic touch
jokes.punchline: Chandler deflates the romance by pointing out Joey already provides this service inadvertently, via his chronic candy hoarding
jokes.explanation: "Rolos everywhere" is a funny, specific detail that makes Joey's slovenliness feel lived-in rather than generic. The joke recontextualizes the romantic hotel moment through the lens of their actual daily life — Monica's happiness is undermined by the mundane truth. Good economy and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, look at these chocolates on the pillow! This is so fancy!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What are you talking about? My apartment looks like this all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, that's not chocolate, that's... I don't even want to know.

jokes.text: Chandler urgently watching a high-speed car chase on TV during their romantic getaway, resisting room changes
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are on a romantic weekend together, meant to be their special escape
jokes.punchline: Chandler is immediately sucked into a TV car chase and treats it as an emergency that trumps the entire romantic premise
jokes.explanation: A reliable but not exceptionally original premise — man addicted to TV during romantic moment. Works because it's sustained and escalates. The specific detail of the car chase gives it texture.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey everyone! Monica and I are going away this weekend!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler! Do you have to announce it to the entire world?

jokes.text: "Oh, dear God! They gave us glasses! The glasses have lipstick on them. Who knows what else they didn't change?"
jokes.setup: Chandler is happy with the first hotel room; Monica immediately finds a flaw
jokes.punchline: Monica spirals from one imperfect glass to a full hygiene catastrophe scenario — perfectly on-brand obsessive-compulsive panic
jokes.explanation: Monica's catastrophizing from a dirty glass to full hotel contamination is very character-specific. The logic follows her OCD spiral in a satisfying arc. Character integration score is high because only Monica gets this joke.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, there's lipstick on this glass! This is disgusting!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, it's a hotel glass.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Exactly! Do you know how many people have used this glass? How many mouths have touched this rim?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Mon, you're staying in a nice hotel.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't care! I looked at the remote control and there's a stain on it I can't identify. A STAIN, Rachel!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Did you check the bedspread?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh God, I'm not even going to look at the bedspread. I'm sleeping in my coat.

jokes.text: "Okay, but let's do it now. Chopper Five just lost its feed!"
jokes.setup: Monica wants to switch rooms to escape the lipstick glass; Chandler is focused on the car chase
jokes.punchline: Chandler agrees to the room switch — but only if they do it immediately so he doesn't miss Chopper Five's coverage. The helicopter losing its feed is treated as a genuine crisis.
jokes.explanation: "Chopper Five just lost its feed" is a funny specific detail — it makes the TV addiction feel real and escalates the running gag. The name "Chopper Five" does real comedic work.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We could change rooms.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Change rooms? Monica, there's helicopter coverage!

jokes.text: "Not again. / This happened when my grandfather died."
jokes.setup: Ross's nose starts bleeding during his emotional confession
jokes.punchline: He volunteers that this also happened at his grandfather's death — revealing a psychosomatic stress response and connecting this moment to that level of grief
jokes.explanation: "Not again" does double work: it's a callback within the scene AND implies a history. The grandfather reveal adds dark poignancy while keeping it funny — it tells us the nosebleed is emotionally triggered, which makes this confession feel as significant as a death to Ross. Smart writing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is that—am I bleeding?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: This always happens! Every time I hear something bad, I just start bleeding from my nose.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's like my body's way of saying 'nope, can't handle this information.'

jokes.text: "They say he's only got half a tank left." / "Half a tank? Still lots of high-speed chasing to do!"
jokes.setup: Chandler is now watching the car chase from a new hotel room
jokes.punchline: He's still fully invested, doing math on the fugitive's remaining fuel as if it's sports statistics
jokes.explanation: The running gag continues to build. Chandler analyzing fuel reserves for a car chase is funny because of his enthusiasm. The gag is now three beats in and gaining momentum.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, I can't see you anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I just... I can't do this.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is it because of my nosebleed? Because I can tilt my head back!

jokes.text: "This has a garden view. We paid for an ocean view. / Our last ocean-view room was unacceptable to you."
jokes.setup: Monica objects to the garden view in the new room; Chandler points out she rejected the ocean view room
jokes.punchline: The irony of Monica complaining about the garden view when she caused the loss of the ocean view is laid bare — classic cringe sitcom logic
jokes.explanation: Functional callback to Monica's earlier perfectionism, now turned against her. Competent but not exceptional — the structure is predictable.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: He's still got a quarter tank. We could chase him for like... two more hours.

jokes.text: "These clowns want to take us for a ride. I won't let them." / "I hear you, Mugsy."
jokes.setup: Chandler has pulled the bellman aside to privately handle the room situation
jokes.punchline: Chandler's private conversation reveals he's going full tough-guy negotiator about hotel rooms — Monica sarcastically calls him "Mugsy," deflating the gangster posturing
jokes.explanation: "Mugsy" is a perfect name drop — it's a classic movie gangster nickname that Monica uses to mock Chandler's tough-guy pretense. The specificity of the name is what makes the joke. Chandler playing hard-boiled over hotel rooms is funny self-inflation.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's not ocean. It's urine.

jokes.text: Chandler pivots mid-sentence from "Just pick one so I can watch the..." to "Have a perfect, magical weekend together with you?"
jokes.setup: Chandler is about to admit he wants to watch TV — the whole point of his room urgency
jokes.punchline: He catches himself and smoothly substitutes "have a perfect, magical weekend together with you" — the cover is hilariously unconvincing given everything that's happened
jokes.explanation: The mid-sentence pivot is excellently structured — the audience sees the correction happening in real time, which is funnier than if he'd said it cleanly. "Perfect, magical weekend" is an absurdly romantic phrase deployed with zero sincerity. Good character and structure scores.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Easy there, Scarface.

jokes.text: "Nothing. It's over. Damn it! This is regularly scheduled programming!"
jokes.setup: Chandler has been frantically monitoring the car chase; Monica asks if they can turn off the TV
jokes.punchline: The car chase ends — but Chandler's devastation at "regularly scheduled programming" is as intense as a personal loss
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the running car-chase gag. "This is regularly scheduled programming!" is a great line — his outrage at normal TV as an affront is funny, and the specificity of the phrase (not 'it's over' but naming the actual replacement content) elevates it. This is the best punchline of the hotel subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I mean, how stupid do you have to be? You're on a high-speed chase and you think you can lose the cops by driving through a residential neighborhood?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, maybe he had a very good reason. Maybe his grandmother just died and he was rushing to the funeral.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, he's a bank robber!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A grieving bank robber.

jokes.text: "Am I getting in the way of the room-switching fun?"
jokes.setup: Monica pushes back on Chandler about the weekend not going well
jokes.punchline: Chandler sardonically implies that the room-switching was Monica's entertainment — reframing her perfectionism as recreational
jokes.explanation: Decent sarcasm. The phrase "room-switching fun" is a good specific Chandler construction. Slight deflation of the Monica-perfectionism gag.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I mean... Mom... nica. Monica. I said Monica.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Did you just call me Mom?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No! No, I said 'Mo-om-nica.' It's a new thing I'm doing with your name. Monica. With emphasis.

jokes.text: "Do not speak ill of the dead." (about the car chase driver who ran out of gas)
jokes.setup: Monica mocks the fugitive driver for running out of gas on a car chase
jokes.punchline: Chandler defends a stranger on TV with the solemnity reserved for a deceased loved one
jokes.explanation: "Do not speak ill of the dead" applied to a TV car chase criminal is a great comic misapplication of gravitas. It's the perfect eulogy beat for the running gag — and it's only six words. Very high economy. The gag fully earns its ending here.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm done. I can't do this anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, technically, you can do it anymore. 'Anymore' means you could continue doing it in the future, but you're choosing not to. If you couldn't do it, you'd say you can't do it 'any longer.'

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm leaving!

jokes.text: "What did you say?" / "I said, 'Jeez, relax, Mon.'"
jokes.setup: Monica heard Chandler call her "Mom" and demands clarification
jokes.punchline: Chandler tries to pass it off as "Mon" — a nickname contraction — which is technically plausible but clearly a desperate cover, and no one believes it
jokes.explanation: The recovery attempt is funnier than the original slip. "Jeez, relax, Mon" is technically a valid reading — Monica's nickname is Mon — which makes the lie almost defensible, which makes it MORE uncomfortable. Chandler's panic driving the cover attempt is perfect character work. The audience knows he's lying; Monica knows he's lying; he knows she knows. This is cringe comedy at its best in this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, LaPooh was really depressed for a while. He just sat there staring at nothing. It was like he'd seen things... terrible things.

jokes.text: You have no idea what a nightmare this has been. This is so hard.
jokes.setup: Ross has just told Rachel she won't see him anymore and seems to expect sympathy
jokes.punchline: His pivot to 'you have no idea what a nightmare THIS has been' — making himself the victim — is the joke, playing into Ross's self-involved obliviousness
jokes.explanation: Very Ross — his self-pity in the moment of delivering bad news to someone else is perfectly in character. The audience recognizes this trait and it lands well, though it's not a constructed joke so much as character-based cringe.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh sure, we can see each other. Like I could see Mr. Whiskers after he died and they put him in that little box.

jokes.text: "Storming out." / "It's your apartment." / "Yeah? Well, that's how mad I am!"
jokes.setup: Rachel has just learned Ross agreed to never see her again; she announces she's storming out in anger
jokes.punchline: Ross points out it's her apartment, so storming out punishes herself. Rachel's response — "That's how mad I am!" — escalates the absurdity by making self-sabotage the measure of her fury
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The three-beat structure is perfect: (1) emotional declaration, (2) logical deflation, (3) escalation that tops both. "That's how mad I am!" is an excellent line because Rachel commits fully to an objectively self-defeating gesture — and that commitment IS the joke. Highly quotable, well-structured, character-specific to Rachel's dramatic personality. Approaches the 8-anchor benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm leaving and I'm taking my stuff with me!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, this is my apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't care! I'm leaving anyway!

jokes.text: "No, I got to see Donald Trump waiting for an elevator."
jokes.setup: Joey asks if Chandler's "conference" weekend was a bust
jokes.punchline: Chandler admits the weekend was bad, then immediately adds this as a silver lining — spotting a celebrity waiting for an elevator is treated as the weekend's consolation prize
jokes.explanation: A topical celebrity name-drop that gets a mild laugh. The specificity of "waiting for an elevator" is what saves it from being totally throwaway — it's mundane and anti-climactic, which is the point. The joke hasn't aged perfectly given Trump's later career, but in context it's functional.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can't believe this! That candy bar ruined everything!

jokes.text: Monica's food poisoning cover story: "Some people don't appreciate good food. Maybe the food tasted good at first... but then made everybody vomit and have diarrhea."
jokes.setup: Monica needs to explain why her culinary fair weekend went badly (to cover the real reason)
jokes.punchline: She concocts an increasingly unflattering account of her own (fictional) cooking causing mass food poisoning — inadvertently destroying her professional reputation in the lie
jokes.explanation: Very Monica — a chef inventing a cover story that involves her food making everyone sick. The escalation from "didn't appreciate it" to full mass food poisoning is funny because Monica's culinary pride is a core character trait, making this self-sabotage especially painful (and funny). "Vomit and have diarrhea" as a punchline is broad but lands.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I saw Donald Trump at the hotel today.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Did you know that Donald Trump's middle name is John? Donald John Trump. I don't know why I know that.

jokes.text: "Fine. $300." / "$300?" / "Just think of it as $25 per room."
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are splitting the bill for their disastrous hotel weekend
jokes.punchline: Chandler reframes the $300 as $25 per room switched — a mathematically accurate but comedically damning breakdown of their chaos
jokes.explanation: "$25 per room" is an excellent callback payoff to the room-switching subplot. It's unexpected math that retroactively quantifies how ridiculous their weekend was. The joke rewards viewers who tracked the room count. High economy — the punchline is six words and contains everything.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Did you know that Donald Trump's apartment building has an elevator with gold plating?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How do you even KNOW that?

jokes.text: "What are you guys woofing about? Chandler stole a 20 from my purse!"
jokes.setup: Joey and Phoebe interrupt Chandler and Monica's argument
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately accuses Chandler of theft — with zero prompting and apparent certainty — as a non-sequitur
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's wild accusation is funny but slightly underdeveloped as written. "Woofing" is a fun Phoebe-ism. The accusation lands as character comedy but the setup-to-punchline structure is weak.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Some people just don't appreciate good food.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, or maybe they just have bad taste buds. I mean, how else do you explain someone not liking pizza? That's like not liking... breathing.

jokes.text: "You know what? Now that I think about it... I constantly find myself without 20s, and you... always have lots."
jokes.setup: Phoebe accuses Chandler of stealing $20; Monica impulsively piles on
jokes.punchline: Monica turns on her own boyfriend by suddenly "realizing" she's always been missing 20-dollar bills — betraying him without evidence in a comedic about-face
jokes.explanation: The rewatch value comes from knowing Monica and Chandler are secretly dating — her turning on him publicly while covering her tracks is an extra layer of comedy for those in the know. The pause before "always have lots" is a timing beat that sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Three hundred dollars?! For one night?!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, if you think about it, we switched rooms four times, so that's really only seventy-five dollars per room.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, that's not how math works.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It works if you don't think about it too hard.

jokes.text: "You got married too fast." / "That's not advice." / "I told you."
jokes.setup: Ross asks Joey for advice about how to handle the Emily/Rachel situation
jokes.punchline: Joey's "advice" is simply a post-mortem diagnosis of the original mistake — not actionable at all. When Ross objects, Joey points out he warned him the advice would be unwelcome.
jokes.explanation: Three-beat structure that fires perfectly. Joey's useless but technically-accurate advice, Ross's correct observation that it's not advice, and Joey's pre-emptive vindication are all in character and efficiently written. "I told you" as the final beat is a perfect button — Joey already said he wouldn't like it, so he's both right and unhelpful simultaneously. High character integration: only Joey gives advice this brazenly useless.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He borrowed twenty dollars from me three months ago and never paid it back!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, I was going to pay you back!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Were you? WERE YOU? Because it seems like you've just decided to steal from me!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh come on, it's twenty dollars!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's not about the money, Chandler. It's about trust. It's about respect. It's about the fact that you clearly don't care about our friendship!

jokes.text: "If anyone asked me to give up any of you, I couldn't do it." / "Me neither." / "Maybe I could do it."
jokes.setup: Joey and Ross share a sincere moment about not being able to give up their friends
jokes.punchline: Chandler quietly breaks from the warmth to admit he could probably manage — his antisocial honesty deflating the sentimental beat
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom anti-sentiment beat. Chandler undermining a sincere moment with his honest self-assessment is perfect to his character — his emotional unavailability played for laughs. The economy is excellent: five words do all the work. The timing (beat after the warmth) is crucial.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I told Rachel that Emily said I had to choose between her and Rachel, and Rachel just stood there with this look of complete horror on her face.

jokes.text: "I know you guys heard about me and Ross. But I've been obsessing about it and would love not to talk about it."
jokes.setup: Rachel enters and addresses the group about the Ross situation
jokes.punchline: She simultaneously acknowledges her obsession AND requests not to discuss it — which is itself discussing it, and the self-awareness makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: A self-aware line that captures Rachel's character — she's dramatic but also occasionally aware of being dramatic. The contradiction is built into the sentence structure.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Your wife doesn't like you.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's not helpful, Joey.

jokes.text: "I don't know if this falls under that category... but Ross is right back there." / "That's not Ross." / "Not that guy. He does look like him, though. Ross is in the bathroom."
jokes.setup: Rachel has just asked not to talk about Ross; Phoebe immediately brings up relevant Ross-adjacent information
jokes.punchline: The confusion about which person is Ross, plus the casual observation that the wrong guy looks like him, delays and deflects the genuine news in an absurd way
jokes.explanation: The accidental stranger who looks like Ross is a good absurdist detail. Phoebe's oblivious violation of Rachel's just-stated wish is very in character. The misdirect works.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I could give up Chandler.

jokes.text: "Oh, my God! It's happening. It's already started. I'm Kip."
jokes.setup: Rachel is upset about being edged out of the friend group
jokes.punchline: She identifies herself as "Kip" — the previous group member who got phased out after a breakup — realizing she's experiencing the same fate
jokes.explanation: "I'm Kip" is a great comedic crystallization of a larger anxiety. The fact that "Kip" is a name the audience just heard for the first time makes it instantly memorable as a concept. Rachel's horror at her own categorization is well-played. The line functions as both emotional truth and joke.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is that Ross? What is he doing here? He always comes on Thursdays!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait... what day is it today?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's Thursday.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh God. Oh God, no. He didn't even call me. He just... came here without telling me.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm becoming the phased-out friend. I'm Chandler's girlfriend's sister!

jokes.text: "Who's Kip?" / "My old roommate. We all hung out together." / "Oh, that poor bastard."
jokes.setup: Rachel references "Kip" and the others explain who he was
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately and sincerely declares him "that poor bastard" — before even hearing what happened to him, just based on the group's tone
jokes.explanation: "That poor bastard" — three words, maximum empathy delivered with deadpan certainty before Joey knows the details. This is Joey at his comedic best: sincere, slightly dim, perfectly timed. The audience laughs at his instinctive pity. Very high economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm moving to Paris. I'm going to become Kip.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Who's Kip?

jokes.text: "I just assumed Phoebe would be the one to go."
jokes.setup: The group is discussing who would get phased out if Rachel leaves
jokes.punchline: Ross casually reveals he had mentally designated Phoebe as the expendable friend — to her face
jokes.explanation: Devastating and funny. Ross saying this out loud — to Phoebe — is the kind of brutal honesty that works in sitcoms because it's what everyone might privately think but would never say. The specificity of Phoebe as the expendable one (peripheral, least connected by blood or history) has an internal logic that makes it land even harder.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, who's Kip?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh man, that's terrible. Poor guy.

jokes.text: "You live far away, you're not related. You lift right out."
jokes.setup: Ross explains his reasoning for thinking Phoebe would be phased out
jokes.punchline: "You lift right out" — a phrase normally used for detachable objects — applied to a human friend's disposability
jokes.explanation: "You lift right out" is the best line of the episode. It's a genuinely original phrase — using the language of modular furniture or Lego pieces to describe human disposability. It's shocking, specific, and perfectly economical. Ross delivers it with the calm logic of someone who has thought this through, which makes it worse (and funnier). This approaches the top of the scale for this episode — the kind of line that gets quoted for years. The image of a person being "lifted out" of a social group like a component is an unexpected and brilliant construction.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, we all agreed we'd phase him out gradually. You know, stop inviting him to things, take longer to return his calls...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: But I feel terrible about it. I mean, the guy was always nice to us.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We basically ghosted him before ghosting was even a thing.

jokes.text: "Someone left an eyelash curler in your room." / "Yes, that was mine." / "I figured you met a girl and she left it." / "That would have made more sense."
jokes.setup: The hotel calls about an eyelash curler left in Chandler's room; Joey assumes a woman left it
jokes.punchline: Chandler admits it was his, then agrees that Joey's explanation "would have made more sense" — inadvertently suggesting the secret relationship is less plausible than a random hookup
jokes.explanation: "That would have made more sense" is an excellent self-aware line — Chandler acknowledging the implausibility of his own situation while simultaneously protecting the secret. The eyelash curler as a plot device is well-chosen. For rewatchers, this is additionally funny knowing the full context.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That was so long ago! Things were completely different back then.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How different?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You had a goatee!

jokes.text: "I don't even feel like I know you anymore." / Joey's reaction to discovering Chandler uses an eyelash curler
jokes.setup: Joey learns Chandler owns and uses an eyelash curler
jokes.punchline: Joey treats this as a fundamental identity crisis — more disturbing than any real revelation would be
jokes.explanation: Joey's masculine bafflement at Chandler's grooming habits is a reliable character beat. "I don't even feel like I know you anymore" applied to an eyelash curler is a slight overreaction that plays well.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm worried that I'm going to be phased out. Like, what if I'm not essential anymore?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, please. You're totally essential.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, I mean, we all are. We're a unit.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Actually, if we're being honest, Phoebe's pretty expendable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? She sings to herself. She makes up her own words. Nobody even knows what she does for a living.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm a masseuse!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: See? Nobody believed you.

jokes.text: "Were you or were you not... on a gay cruise?"
jokes.setup: Joey promises to believe whatever Chandler says about the weekend; he's going to ask one question
jokes.punchline: His one question — the culmination of all his suspicion — is whether Chandler was on a gay cruise
jokes.explanation: "Gay cruise" as the conclusion of Joey's detective work is a great absurd leap. The build-up — "whatever you say I'll believe you," the gravity of the moment — makes the specific, left-field accusation land harder. The pause before the question is key. For rewatchers, this is additionally funny because the truth (a secret romantic weekend with Monica) is simultaneously more and less dramatic than a gay cruise.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes, that's mine. I use it. Problem?

jokes.text: "You got to come with me. Where? Wherever I go. You and me, we'll start a new group. We're the best ones." / "Okay, but try to get Joey too."
jokes.setup: Phoebe tells Rachel she should leave with her to form a new friend group
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately starts negotiating membership — specifically requesting Joey, implicitly ranking him above others
jokes.explanation: "We're the best ones" from Phoebe is funny because it comes from genuine delusion. Rachel's immediate pivot to recruitment strategy is in character. The warmth of the scene plus the absurdity of the plan makes this land.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Chandler uses an eyelash curler? An eyelash curler?! What is happening to the world? What's next, he's gonna tell me he uses a deep conditioning mask? That he plucks his eyebrows? I mean, come on, man, where does it end? When did taking care of yourself become so... so complicated?

jokes.text: You got to come with me. / Where? / Wherever I go. / You and me, we'll start a new group. We're the best ones.
jokes.setup: Phoebe feels bad about Chandler's earlier comment that she'd be the first phased out.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's solution is to preemptively form a splinter group with Rachel — declaring them 'the best ones' with absolute conviction.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's solution being to immediately start a new friend group — with herself in charge of declaring who is 'the best ones' — is very on-brand. Her cheerful self-aggrandizement is consistent character work.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, where do you go every weekend? You're always sneaking off somewhere.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not sneaking off. I told you, I have a conference.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A conference? Yeah, right. I know what's really going on.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You're training to be a secret agent! Or wait—you're a spy! No, no, no... you're building a robot in a warehouse somewhere!

jokes.text: "Plenty of people just see their sisters at Thanksgiving... their college roommates at reunions... and Joey at Burger King."
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to comfort Rachel (and himself) by normalizing the idea of drifting apart
jokes.punchline: The list descends from 'sister at Thanksgiving' (traditional) to 'college roommate at reunion' (acceptable) to 'Joey at Burger King' (absurdly specific and bleak)
jokes.explanation: "Joey at Burger King" is a genuinely excellent line — it escalates by getting progressively more mundane and sad, culminating in an image so specific and bleak that it's both funny and devastating. The list structure is perfect: each element slightly worse than the last, with the final item being an unplanned, coincidental fast food encounter with one of your closest friends. This is the second-best joke in the episode. High quotability, high structure, high economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm gonna go. I'm gonna leave you two alone. And if I never see you again, I want you to know that you meant the world to me.

jokes.text: "First, I'd have said the right name at my wedding."
jokes.setup: Ross sincerely asks Rachel what she would do if she were in his position
jokes.punchline: Rachel's first suggestion is not to have caused the whole situation by saying her name at the altar — delivered as practical advice, not emotional recrimination
jokes.explanation: A devastating callback delivered with perfect economy. Rachel answers Ross's sincere question with a critique disguised as practical advice — "First, I'd have said the right name" implies a list of steps to follow, then stops there because it's the only relevant step. The structure is impeccable, and the character integration is high because only Rachel can deliver this specific wound. Among the top three jokes of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't know, Ross. I mean, what would you do? Oh wait, I know — you'd say the wrong name at the altar!

jokes.text: Joey walking in and immediately offering a fake cover story: "Sorry to interrupt, but Phoebe said you want to talk to me about a trip?" Then seeing the emotional scene and retreating: "I just came over to drop off... nothing."
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel are having an emotional, private conversation; Joey walks in with a terrible cover story Phoebe apparently sent him with
jokes.punchline: He reads the room, abandons the excuse, and says he came to drop off "nothing" — a perfect Joey retreat
jokes.explanation: "I just came over to drop off... nothing" is a beautiful Joey moment — his social intelligence occasionally outpaces his verbal intelligence, and when he reads the emotional room, the best he can do is acknowledge the fiction mid-sentence. The ellipsis before "nothing" is crucial to the timing. Very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're saying fights don't end relationships?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Because I've been doing this all wrong. I thought one argument and you're supposed to break up.

jokes.text: Sorry to interrupt, but Phoebe said you want to talk to me about a trip?
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel are having a deeply emotional, painful conversation about their friendship ending.
jokes.punchline: Joey wanders in having been told by Phoebe — entirely fictitiously — that Rachel wanted to discuss a trip, completely interrupting the most emotionally charged scene in the episode.
jokes.explanation: Joey's oblivious interruption of a painful moment is structurally correct sitcom timing — using physical comedy of situation to provide emotional relief. The added beat that Phoebe engineered the interruption by lying to Joey about a 'trip' makes it funnier and raises questions about Phoebe's motives.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, so you and Rachel had a fight. That doesn't mean anything is wrong with your relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Grown-ups fight. It's normal. It's healthy, even.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What matters is that you talk about it, you work through it, and you come out the other side stronger.

jokes.text: "Why exactly?" / "Because of the weekend. We had a fight." / "Chandler, that's crazy. If you always gave up after a fight, you'd never be with anyone longer than—"
jokes.setup: Chandler assumes the relationship is over because they had a rough weekend
jokes.punchline: Monica begins a lecture about not giving up after fights — and then catches herself, since she's describing a pattern that applies to her as well
jokes.explanation: The cut-off sentence is well-structured — Monica's self-aware stop implies she was about to describe her own relationship history, which would undermine her point. The implication is funnier than any explicit completion would be.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Are we in a relationship?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I guess so.

jokes.text: Chandler's realization: "This isn't over?" / Monica: "You are so cute!"
jokes.setup: Monica has been explaining that fights are normal in relationships; Chandler slowly processes this
jokes.punchline: Chandler's earnest, almost childlike surprise at learning fights don't end relationships — and Monica's warm, amused response — reveals the depth of his emotional inexperience
jokes.explanation: Chandler's emotional unavailability and fear of commitment are core character traits, so his genuine surprise at relationship norms lands as both funny and endearing. Monica calling him cute is the right response. Character integration is high.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's like, you know, I got this thing inside me, and I gotta keep it in. It's like I'm holding in a fart at a fancy dinner.

jokes.text: "Welcome to an adult relationship."
jokes.setup: Monica has just talked Chandler through the basic concept that couples fight and stay together
jokes.punchline: She formally welcomes him to adult relationships — framing basic emotional maturity as a milestone achievement
jokes.explanation: "Welcome to an adult relationship" is a great line — Monica conferring a certificate on Chandler for understanding the most basic relationship concept. It's condescending and warm simultaneously, which is very Monica. The formal "welcome" construction is funny and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey knows.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? No, he doesn't!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He does. He figured it out.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How could he figure it out? We've been so careful!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, you guys want some gum?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: GUM?! Why would he offer us gum? Is that code? Did he mean something else by gum? Oh God, he knows everything!

jokes.text: "We're in a relationship?" / Monica: "I'm afraid so."
jokes.setup: Monica says "welcome to an adult relationship"
jokes.punchline: Chandler questions whether they're even in a relationship — still not entirely sure what's happening — and Monica confirms it with resigned affection
jokes.explanation: "I'm afraid so" is a perfect Monica line — she's not thrilled about being in a relationship with someone this emotionally stunted, but she's in it. Chandler's question revealing he hadn't processed this basic fact of his life is excellent character comedy. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, here we go. 'To play tennis, first you need a Phoebe.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: 'Then you need a Phoebe and a Phoebe.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: 'You hit the Phoebe over the Phoebe, and your opponent tries to Phoebe it back.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: 'If the Phoebe lands outside the Phoebe, it's a Phoebe.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: 'The first player to win six Phoebes wins the Phoebe.'

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm a sport now?

jokes.text: "Can I use your eyelash curler? I lost mine." / Monica: "It's in the bathroom."
jokes.setup: Earlier in the episode, Chandler's eyelash curler was exposed as suspicious evidence of a secret companion
jokes.punchline: Rachel asks to borrow Monica's eyelash curler — which IS the same one Chandler left at the hotel, now back in Monica's bathroom, connecting the dots for the audience
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback for attentive viewers — the eyelash curler's journey from hotel room to Monica's bathroom quietly confirms she was with him. Monica's flat "It's in the bathroom" doesn't betray anything, which is itself funny. Rewatch value is high because on second viewing the entire exchange is loaded.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait! You can't just leave! We haven't finished the Mad Libs properly!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, it's just a game.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's just a game?! It's a SYSTEM! You need an adjective, then a noun, then a verb! There's an ORDER to these things!

jokes.text: Joey discovers Monica and Chandler are together: "You? And you? But you cannot tell anyone. No one knows. But how? When? It happened in London. In London!"
jokes.setup: Joey has figured out or been told about Monica and Chandler's relationship
jokes.punchline: Joey's reaction is a cascade of shocked questions, each answered before he fully processes the last one — "In London!" as a final exclamation treating the location as the most shocking detail
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Joey's reaction is well-structured — each beat of shock followed by another question before the last answer registers. "In London!" as the punchline works because it treats the city as the punchiest revelation, implying Joey is most scandalized by the geography. His genuine shock and delight are very Joey.

jokes.text: "But it is a big deal! I have to tell someone!" / "You can't."
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler ask Joey to keep their relationship secret
jokes.punchline: Joey's immediate instinct is that this secret is too good to keep — his loyalty and his social impulses are in direct conflict
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat — Joey's inability to contain information is a known trait. Not particularly clever writing but it plays well off his reaction.

jokes.text: "I don't want to see that!" (Joey reacting to Monica and Chandler kissing or being affectionate)
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler confirm their relationship to Joey
jokes.punchline: Joey's visceral objection to seeing his two friends be romantic — despite having just been told about and apparently supportive of their relationship
jokes.explanation: Joey accepting the relationship intellectually but recoiling from witnessing it physically is a funny distinction. "I don't want to see that!" is a great reaction line — high economy for a physical gag.

jokes.text: "We're so stupid. Do you know what's going on in there? They're trying to take Joey!"
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler realize Rachel and Phoebe are with Joey — the friends who know their secret
jokes.punchline: They frame the social situation as an active heist to "take Joey" — as if he's a territory being claimed
jokes.explanation: "They're trying to take Joey" treats friendship like a custody dispute. The absurdity of framing Joey as a contested resource is funny. Good paranoia beat for the secret-couple subplot.

jokes.text: Mad Libs: "The most popular Phoebe in tennis is called the overhand Phoebe." / "If you win, slap your opponent on the Phoebe and say, 'Hi, Phoebe'!"
jokes.setup: Joey and Phoebe are playing Mad Libs while trapped in the apartment; Phoebe has apparently filled in "Phoebe" for every blank
jokes.punchline: The resulting Mad Libs sentences use "Phoebe" as a noun replacing every word — producing absurdist, surreal sentences that are funny both as wordplay and as an expression of Phoebe's self-centeredness
jokes.explanation: "Slap your opponent on the Phoebe" is genuinely funny — the sentence structure still makes grammatical sense while being entirely nonsensical in meaning. It's a callback to the survival kit and a showcase for Phoebe's lovably narcissistic world view. The Mad Libs device is perfectly suited for a sitcom payoff.

jokes.text: "That's cute. We really all enjoyed it. But it doesn't count. / For what? / Just count in our heads as good Mad Libs."
jokes.setup: Joey and Rachel are evaluating Phoebe's Mad Libs answers
jokes.punchline: They invent an entirely undefined standard for Mad Libs validity — "count in our heads" — which is both condescending and meaningless
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny coda to the Mad Libs bit. The notion of Mad Libs that "count in our heads" is sufficiently absurd. Weaker than the sentences themselves.

jokes.text: "Guys, rules are good! Rules help control the fun."
jokes.setup: Joey and Rachel are leaving; Phoebe wants to continue the Mad Libs properly
jokes.punchline: Phoebe defends rule-following for a game of Mad Libs with the gravity of someone defending social order — "Rules help control the fun" is a hilariously anti-fun statement about fun
jokes.explanation: "Rules help control the fun" is a great closing line — it's paradoxical, self-undermining, and perfectly in character for Phoebe's idiosyncratic logic. It's also broadly applicable enough to be quotable in real life. The delivery of this as a sincere belief (not ironic) is what makes it land. High economy — the sentence contradicts itself in five words.

tmdb_overview: Monica and Chandler plan an Atlantic City getaway in order to have an intimate weekend away from their friends.  Meanwhile, Ross prepares himself to tell Rachel that he can't see her anymore.
insight: Steady character work carries a middle-tier episode through observational humor without standout moments.
